metadata.title: Motivational Profile, Future Expectations, and Attitudes toward Study of Secondary School Students in Spain: Results of the PISA Report 2018
metadata.venue: Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses microdata from the PISA 2018 assessment for Spain, drawing students in compulsory secondary education (mean age 15.83). The manuscript describes that analyses were conducted on the PISA 2018 database made available by the Ministry of Education and Vocational Training and INEE, but it does not report whether complex survey sampling weights were applied. Because the reported analyses are chi-square tests, multinomial logistic regression, and structural equation modeling (AMOS/SPSS), the paper does not document any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedure. As a result, the weighting strategy for producing population-representative estimates is unclear from the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are categorical survey responses (reasons for studying/not studying, and future expectations categories) and related attitude/influence items, not cognitive achievement scores with PISA plausible values. Therefore, PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcomes. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap because analytic samples in survey datasets typically require explicit treatment of missing questionnaire responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student-level data for Spain, restricted to compulsory secondary education students (mean age 15.83) and to specific questionnaire/placement-test items: student standardized gender and age; country of birth for student and parents; grade repetition; reasons for studying/not studying; future expectations (5 years); and influences on future expectations. The paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the described item selection, and it does not specify any missing-response exclusion or imputation rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Spain (compulsory secondary education) — questionnaire items on reasons for studying and future expectations
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multinomial logistic regression: model χ2(50)=1042.79, p=0.000; Nagelkerke R2=0.209 (Cox & Snell R2=0.194). Significant predictors reported in Table 7 include grade repetition, not being interested in content, never studying, grades importance levels, and subject mastery levels (odds ratios with 95% CI; significance indicated by * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged grade repetition, not being interested in content, never studying, and influences on future expectations (grades importance and subject mastery) to predict students’ future expectations categories (e.g., studying requiring a degree vs. working). The multinomial model was statistically significant and explained about 20.9% of the variability (Nagelkerke R2=0.209), indicating that motivational discouragement and school-performance-related influences are meaningfully associated with adolescents’ future plans. This indicates that strengthening engagement and improving perceived academic competence may shift students away from lower-credential future pathways, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (N=35,943; mean age 15.83) focusing on compulsory secondary students’ motivational reasons for studying/not studying and their future expectations for 5 years ahead. The paper reports descriptive chi-square associations by sex and grade repetition, then estimates a multinomial logistic regression to predict future-expectation categories from sex, grade repetition, discouraging reasons (not interested in content; never studying), and influences on expectations (school grades and subject mastery). The final multinomial model was significant (χ2(50)=1042.79, p<0.001) with Nagelkerke R2=0.209, and Table 7 reports odds ratios and confidence intervals for multiple outcome categories. Finally, a structural equation model (maximum likelihood estimation) reports good fit indices (e.g., IFI=0.994, RMSEA=0.017) and a pathway where grade repetition predicts discouragement reasons, which in turn relate to future expectations. Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight use and missing-data handling, and the fact that the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the manuscript includes predictive modeling language (multinomial logistic regression and structural equation modeling), it does not implement machine-learning algorithms as defined in the extraction schema (no ML learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM/NN are reported). Consequently, ml_techniques is left empty and plausible-values handling is set to not_applicable because the outcomes are categorical questionnaire responses rather than PV-based achievement scores.
